newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin speech seen long on style, short on content.
newsitem.headline: Jospin speech seen long on style, short on content.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, caught between expansive campaign pledges and a fragile economy, will offer quick, inexpensive promises and avoid tough tasks in a policy speech on Thursday, economists said.

Jospin, whose Socialist party won control of the National Assembly this month after promising to curb austerity and to fuel the economy by boosting consumer purchasing power, is hemmed in by the need to cut public deficits to qualify France for a single European currency in January 1999.
He is also constrained by a promise not to raise taxes or overall spending in pursuit of his expansionary aims. He is to make his policy speech to the National Assembly at 1300 GMT.
"We think he will focus on gestures that have a big political impact but little budgetary impact," said Marie Owens-Thomsen, chief economist at BIP in Paris.

She said these would probably include raising the minimum wage by four to eight percent, a cut in the lowest Value Added Tax (VAT) (sales tax) rate and a civil service pay hike of two percent in September.

These measures, which would be popular and allow Jospin to say he was keeping his campaign promises, would cost a relatively modest 10 billion francs ($1.7 billion), and could be financed with minimum spending cuts in other areas, economists said.
"We're not talking about a very big wage bill increase because this only concerns 1.5 million people, or about 2.2 million in a broader interpretation," said Eric Muller, economist at UBS.
The minimum wage, currently 6,406 francs a month, is due for its annual revision on July 1.
Economists said that beyond such easy to enact measures, which might be put in place by decree, they do not expect to learn much about the new government's domestic economic plan.

"I expect he will restate broad goals, I doubt we will get much detail on the way he is thinking about shortening the workweek," said Bernard Godement, economist at Daiwa. "That goes as well for the jobs creation, the famous 700,000."
The Socialists' most ambitious promises were to create 700,000 jobs in France over the next two to three years and to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 over five years.
Despite sound fundamentals, the French economy continues to stagnate as weak consumer demand and low confidence delays an investment led recovery which economists say is long overdue.

"The macroeconomic situation for an investment-led rebound have never been better. Interest rates are low...companies have lots of cash, trade continues to boom, plus there have been five years of under investing so we should reach a critical mass soon," said Owens-Thomsen.

The government said it will hold an audit of public finances and enact a mini-budget in the autumn, giving itself time to decide how to meet its promise to spur interior demand without overheating the economy.

Despite working hard to lower expectations of immediate progress, pressure to make good on the pledge is likely to be intense. One in every eight active adults in France is out of work and most private economists forecasts are that things will get worse before they get better.
Godement said Jospin would save announcements on how he will tackle unemployment for later in the year, when he is negotiating with unions and other social partners.
"Apart from the minimum wage, where he is bound by time, why should he waste his ammunition," he said. ($ = 5.823 French Francs)
